language_wrapper: Given positive integers {alpha}, {modulus}, and {residue} with 0 <= {residue} < {modulus}, consider only those positive integers n satisfying n ≡ {residue} (mod {modulus}). Determine the least positive integer k for which the equation floor({alpha}/n) = k has no solutions with n constrained by this congruence.
hardness_rationale: This family generalizes the AIME seed by restricting n to a fixed residue class modulo a small modulus. The seed reduces to checking when the interval (N/(k+1), N/k] contains any integer, yielding a simple difference of two floors. Here, one must assess when that interval contains an integer in a specified arithmetic progression, which requires counting lattice points in congruence classes within moving intervals. The minimal k is characterized by the first equality in a derived sequence of counts F(floor(N/k)) − F(floor(N/(k+1))), where F counts numbers in a residue class up to a bound. This introduces subtler boundary behavior and necessitates modular interval counting, a more advanced technique than the original single-floor monotonicity. The verifier enforces instances where the restriction meaningfully changes the minimal k and keeps it near the square-root transition, avoiding trivial cases.
notes: The key computation uses an open-closed interval (N/(k+1), N/k]; counting integers congruent to r mod m in such intervals can be reduced to differences of counts up to integer floors. Ensure alpha is sufficiently large to avoid degenerate k, and keep modulus in a small range to balance existence and difficulty. The generator rejects cases where the congruence does not change the minimal k relative to the unrestricted problem.
source_question: Find the least positive integer $k$ for which the equation $\left\lfloor\frac{2002}{n}\right\rfloor=k$ has no integer solutions for $n$ . (The notation $\lfloor x\rfloor$ means the greatest integer less than or equal to $x$ .)
